rv.q: Four decades later, Swinton remains an electrifying presence.
Swinton’s command of the stage together with Unwin’s clever direction keep the pacing from lagging.
Tilda Swinton has still got it.
The performer’s verbal flexibility and perfect pacing make Man To Man compelling theatre.
Though all the choices here feel calculated to drag this play into 2026, it still doesn't quite make sense now.
The return of chameleonic arthouse darling and Oscar-winner Tilda Swinton to the stage... is a major event. It's also, surprisingly, a little bit boring.
But Karge’s overextended portrait of a woman who could be a modern Mother Courage becomes a test of endurance.

A powerful image of working-class female resilience, Ella/Max survives all these changes in a 85-minute show whose structure is 28 short episodic scenes, written as a mix of declaration, chatter, verse and prose, with brief blasts of songs.
Swinton’s performance feels every bit as powerful as its reputation suggests, making this revival a rare opportunity to witness a landmark production that still has plenty to say.
A play written in the 1980s speaks loudly today and makes another fine addition to the Royal Court’s 70th anniversary season.
Really brave, engaging and emotive performance from Tilda Swinton.
It's an alluring performance that moulds itself around a challenging script.

The show, impressively performed by Tilda Swinton and directed by Stephen Unwin, moves intensely through different scenes, which can be easy to miss, but we still get the picture of a difficult world that is again ambling towards dangerous times.
It is a captivating solo show, with Swinton holding the audience’s attention in her palms.
What is clear is the extraordinary symbiosis between text and performer.
This is clearly the play of the year, both because and despite the fact that it troubles me.
Swinton is mesmerising to watch, whether in complete repose or marching about the stage with a red drinks bottle in her hand, menacing the audience with it.
She moves between vulgarity, humour, fear and sudden flashes of tenderness with astonishing control.
Man to Man is a beautifully told story; one just wonders how to engage with the material if there isn't a direct political point to take a stance on.
Driven by Swinton's expertise, Man to Man is a haunting theatrical feat.
Demanding but richly rewarding, it's not to be missed.

cn.t: Critics praise Tilda Swinton's mesmerizing return to the stage after 39 years, though they're divided on whether Manfred Karge's 1987 monologue about gender identity still resonates today. Her performance captivates; the play itself proves more divisive.
